title: Numbers — and ten shapes you don't know yet
goal: Read and write Persian digits, give a phone number, count things, and use ordinals (first, second, third).
bekal: recognize the ten Persian digits ۰ to ۹ and how they differ from Arabic ones
say numbers into the thousands and read out a phone number
use ordinals for floors, units, and order

dialogs.title: گفتگو — خریدِ سیم‌کارت
dialogs.intro: Budi walks into a phone shop in a mall to buy a SIM card.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: Hello, sir. I'd like a SIM card.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: Here you are. How much is it?

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.id: A hundred and fifty thousand tomans.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: How many gigs of data does it have?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: خوب است. شمارهٔ من چه می‌شود؟
lines.baca: khub ast. shomâre-ye man che mishavad?
lines.id: Good. What will my number be?
lines.literal: good is. number-of I what becomes?

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.text: صفر نهصد و دوازده، سه چهار پنج، شش هفت هشت نه.
lines.baca: sefr nohsad o davâzdah, se chahâr panj, shesh haft hasht noh.

lines.text: ۰۹۱۲ ـ ۳۴۵ ـ ۶۷۸۹. رویِ کارت هم نوشته است.
lines.baca: sefr noh yek do, se chahâr panj, shesh haft hasht noh. ru-ye kârt ham neveshte ast.

lines.text: ممنون. مغازهٔ شما در طبقهٔ چندم است؟
lines.baca: mamnun. maghâze-ye shomâ dar tabaghe-ye chandom ast?

lines.text: طبقهٔ دوم. ولی ما شعبهٔ اول هم داریم.
lines.baca: tabaghe-ye dovvom. vali mâ sho'be-ye avval ham dârim.

lines.literal: floor-of second. but we branch-of first also have-we.

lines.id: Thanks a lot. Do you have a business card?

lines.text: بله، بفرمایید. شمارهٔ ما آخرش سه صفر است.
lines.baca: bale, befarmâyid. shomâre-ye mâ âkharash se sefr ast.

notes: ⚠️ **Persian digits are not Arabic digits, even though they look alike.** Three of them have different shapes: **۴** (four, Arabic ٤), **۵** (five, Arabic ٥), **۶** (six, Arabic ٦). If you have learned the digits used in Arabic, these three are the ones that will trip you up — and, unluckily, they turn up all the time in prices and phone numbers.

**Two lifesavers: دوباره لطفاً and آهسته‌تر.** You will use them more than any other phrase in this book, especially when people say numbers. Nobody minds; Iranians repeat numbers for each other all the time too.

**The "and" (و) between tens and units is always said.** بیست و یک ("twenty-one"), صد و پنجاه ("a hundred and fifty"), هزار و نهصد ("one thousand nine hundred"). Inside numbers it is pronounced *o*, not *va*.

***Tabaghe-ye chandom?*** **(طبقهٔ چندم؟) = "which floor?"** The ending ـم makes ordinals: دو → دوم ("second"), سه → سوم ("third"). The question word چندم ("which number, -th") is different from چند ("how many"). English has no single word for it; think "the how-many-th floor?"
⚠️ **"First" is irregular.** It is not یکم but **اول** (*avval*), an Arabic loanword. یکم does exist, but only for dates (یکمِ مهر). For ordinary order, always use اول.

**Spoken Tehran forms:** قیمتش چنده؟ (*ghymatash chande?*), چند گیگ داره؟ (*chand gig dâre?*), طبقهٔ چندمه؟ (*tabaghe-ye chandome?*). Once again است turns into ـه — the pattern you will meet most often, and the quickest way to sound natural.

grammars.title: The ten Persian digits
body: Persian numbers are written **left to right**, even though the letters run right to left. ۱۳۹۸ reads as usual: one thousand three hundred ninety-eight. It is the only part of Persian writing that runs the other way, and your brain will get used to it within a day.
after: Compare the first two columns closely: **۴ ۵ ۶** versus **٤ ٥ ٦**. Those three are the only shapes you need to relearn; the other seven are identical.
⚠️ Note also that **نه** means "nine" **and** "no". The only difference is stress and tone: نه "nine" is flat, نه "no" is sharper and often drawn out. Context almost always tells them apart.
In Iran today, Western digits (0-9) are also widely used on prices, street signs, and phones. You need to read both, but you can write with either.

grammars.title: Numbers into the thousands
after: **Tens and units are joined with و**, pronounced *o*: بیست و یک (21), چهل و پنج (45), نود و نه (99).
**Hundreds:** دویست (200), سیصد (300), چهارصد (400), پانصد (500), ششصد (600), هفتصد (700), هشتصد (800), نهصد (900). Note that 200 and 500 are irregular — دویست, not دوصد; پانصد, not پنج‌صد.
**Above a thousand:** ده هزار (10,000), صد هزار (100,000), یک میلیون (1,000,000). Since prices in Iran often run into the hundreds of thousands, هزار will be the word you hear most at the checkout.
⚠️ **After a number, the noun stays singular:** five book (پنج کتاب), twenty day (بیست روز), a hundred person (صد نفر). Never add ـها after a number.

grammars.title: Ordinal numbers
after: The rule: **add ـم to the ordinary number.** Three don't quite follow it: اول (not یکم), دوم (from دو, with a double v), سوم (from سه).
Ordinals stand **after** the noun, linked by ezafe: طبقهٔ دوم ("the second floor"), روزِ اول ("the first day"), بارِ آخر ("the last time").
There is also a second form ending in ـمین that stands **before** the noun: دومین بار ("the second time"), اولین روز ("the first day"). Same meaning; this form feels more emphatic.

blocks.text: **The word تا is an all-purpose counter** for any object: دو تا کتاب، سه تا سیب، چند تا؟ It isn't required — دو کتاب is also correct — but in conversation it is almost always there. For people, use نفر: سه نفر، چند نفر؟

blocks.title: Numbers that mean something in Iran
items: **Emergency numbers:** police **۱۱۰**, ambulance **۱۱۵**, fire brigade **۱۲۵**. These three are worth memorizing before you travel.

**Thirteen (۱۳)** is unlucky in Iran, as in many countries, and there is a special holiday to "throw out" its bad luck: سیزده‌بدر (*sizdah-bedar*, "thirteen out"), the thirteenth day of the Persian New Year, when the whole country goes out for a picnic. You'll meet it again in unit 12.

**Forty (۴۰, چهل)** shows up in many sayings and places: چهلم (the memorial on the fortieth day after a death), چهل‌ستون ("forty columns", a famous palace in Isfahan that actually has twenty — the other twenty are their reflection in the pool).

blocks.title: Four phrases for surviving numbers
items: "Once more, please." — دوباره لطفاً. *dobâre lotfan.*
"Slower, please." — آهسته‌تر لطفاً. *âheste-tar lotfan.*
"Digit by digit, please." — رقم به رقم لطفاً. *raghm be raghm lotfan.*
"Could you write it down, please?" — می‌نویسید لطفاً؟ *minevisid lotfan?* This last one solves nine out of ten number problems, and nobody minds writing it down for you.
